scenes.title: Introducing the Curve and Secant Line
scenes.visual: Draw a set of 2D Cartesian axes with a smooth curved function, y = x^2, drawn in blue. Place two distinct points, A and B, on the curve with a red line segment connecting them (the secant line). Below the graph, display the title text 'Average Rate of Change' in white.
scenes.narration: To find how fast a function changes between two points, we draw a secant line connecting them. The slope of this line represents the average rate of change over that interval.

scenes.title: Approaching the Limit
scenes.visual: Keep the axes and the blue curve. Point A remains stationary while Point B slowly moves along the curve toward Point A. The red secant line continuously updates its angle to stay connected to both points, while a right triangle appears below the line showing delta y and delta x shrinking.
scenes.narration: As we bring the second point closer and closer to the first, the interval shrinks. We are looking at the average rate of change over smaller and smaller windows.

scenes.title: The Tangent Line and Derivative
scenes.visual: Point B merges into Point A. The red secant line transforms into a bright yellow line touching the curve at exactly one point (the tangent line). Text at the top updates from 'Secant Line' to 'Tangent Line = Instantaneous Rate of Change', and the derivative formula 'f'(x) = lim (delta x -> 0)' appears next to the point.
scenes.narration: At the limit, as the distance between the points reaches zero, the secant line becomes the tangent line. Its slope is the derivative: the exact instantaneous rate of change at that single point.
